12.text: The Chukchee are fond of singing, especially on ceremonial days. Every

13.text: family, and even every individual, has several songs of his own. Some of

16.text: the civilized ear. The Chukchee are likewise sensitive to the melodiousness

17.text: of a fine voice; and the people often gather in the house of some young

18.text: shaman, known not so much for his skill as for his pleasing voice, to enjoy

23.text: Cleanliness. — The Chukchee cannot be called a clean people, at least
23.note: Printed as a run-in small-cap heading (CLEANLINESS.); flattened to title case, per the same small-cap-flattening convention used for running titles.

24.text: from a civilized point of view. They eat their own lice (Plate XX, Fig. 3),

25.text: wash with urine, and allow the dogs to lick out their dishes. They consume

26.text: the large larvæ of the reindeer-fly, and in summer the herdsmen occasionally

27.text: consume even reindeer-dung mixed with young leaves of various plants. Habits

28.text: of cleanliness, however, are liable to be considered from different standpoints.

29.text: For instance, many of my native acquaintances strongly objected to cow’s milk

30.text: on account of the unclean ways of the animal that yields it. They asserted
30.note: Machine text read 'vields'; the raster clearly shows 'yields' (zoomed via the 29-31 contact sheet).

31.text: also that beef has a peculiar and unpleasant odor, similar to that of cow-dung,

32.text: and some of them even refused to enter the room where beef was being cooked.

33.text: On the other hand, when we objected to the odor of seal-meat, they, in their

34.text: turn, would say, “The seal is quite clean. It washes itself continually in clean

35.text: water. Why do you not object rather to the meat of your own filthy animals?”

36.text: Diseases. — Contagious diseases have repeatedly made their appearance
36.note: Printed as a run-in small-cap heading (DISEASES.); flattened to title case, same convention as line 23.

37.text: among the Chukchee. Small-pox has several times ravaged the population

38.text: of northeastern Siberia. Its latest outbreaks were on the Lower Kolyma in

39.text: 1884, and on the Middle Kolyma in 1889; though the latter epidemic affected

40.text: chiefly the Russians and the Yakut, and had little effect on the Chukchee.
